items.stem: Define the term "in-group favouritism".
items.answer: The tendency to favour members of one's own group over members of out-groups
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the tendency to favour members of one's own group over members of out-groups. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why people show in-group favouritism even in minimal groups.
items.answer: According to social identity theory, categorisation alone creates a social identity; to maintain positive self-esteem, people seek positive distinctiveness for their group, so they favour it even when groups are trivial and there is no conflict (Tajfel et al., 1971).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: According to social identity theory, categorisation alone creates a social identity; to maintain positive self-esteem, people seek positive distinctiveness for their group, so they favour it even when groups are trivial and there is no conflict (Tajfel et al., 1971). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain what the study by Cialdini et al. (1976) suggests about social identity and self-esteem.
items.answer: Findings: students wore more university clothing after wins and were more likely to say "we won" than "we lost". Link: these results are evidence about social identity and self-esteem.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for accurate findings (students wore more university clothing after wins and were more likely to say "we won" than "we lost"); remaining marks for explicitly explaining what the findings show about social identity and self-esteem (not just restating them).

items.stem: Briefly describe football fans after a derby and explain what it reveals about social identity theory.
items.answer: After their team wins a derby in Buenos Aires, fans wear club shirts to work and say "we won"; after a loss, they say "they lost". Fans bask in reflected glory to enhance self-esteem through the in-group and distance themselves after failure, consistent with Cialdini et al. (1976)
items.markingKey: Context (After their team wins a derby in Buenos Aires, fans wear club shirts to work and say "we won"; after a loss, they say "they lost".) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. (1976) – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to social identity theory.

items.stem: A student claims: "Social identity theory says group conflict always requires competition for resources." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: That is realistic conflict theory; SIT holds that categorisation alone can produce in-group favouritism (minimal groups).
items.markingKey: That is realistic conflict theory; SIT holds that categorisation alone can produce in-group favouritism (minimal groups). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A company in Melbourne merges two teams who see each other as rivals. Using social identity theory, suggest one way to reduce in-group favouritism.
items.answer: Create a superordinate, shared identity (new team name, common goals) so former out-group members become in-group members (recategorisation, the common in-group identity model).
items.markingKey: Create a superordinate, shared identity (new team name, common goals) so former out-group members become in-group members (recategorisation, the common in-group identity model).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Social identity theory explains why people discriminate against out-groups."
items.answer: SIT explains in-group favouritism well, but other factors (competition, norms, personality) are needed to explain hostility.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: minimal group studies (Tajfel et al., 1971); BIRGing (Cialdini et al., 1976). Arguments against: in-group favouritism does not always mean out-group hostility; minimal group studies are artificial; cultural variation in group processes (Wetherell, 1982). Supported judgement: SIT explains in-group favouritism well, but other factors (competition, norms, personality) are needed to explain hostility.

items.stem: Using Tajfel et al. (1971) as supporting evidence, explain social categorisation and in-group favouritism.
items.answer: Tajfel et al. (1971). Aim: to investigate whether being categorised into a group is enough to produce in-group favouritism. Method: 64 boys aged 14-15 from a school in Bristol were told they were in a group based on preference for paintings by Klee or Kandinsky (actually random), then allocated points to anonymous in-group and out-group members using matrices. Findings: boys favoured their in-group and often chose maximum difference between groups rather than maximum joint profit Link: social categorisation and in-group favouritism.

items.stem: Outline the aim and method of Bandura (1965).
items.answer: Aim: to investigate whether the consequences to a model affect children's imitation of aggression. Method: Children watched a film of an adult behaving aggressively towards a Bobo doll and being rewarded, punished or receiving no consequences; they were then observed, and later offered incentives to reproduce the model's behaviour.

items.stem: Using Bandura, Ross and Ross (1961) as supporting evidence, explain observational learning of aggression.
items.answer: Bandura, Ross and Ross (1961). Aim: to investigate whether children would imitate aggressive behaviour shown by an adult model. Method: 72 children aged 3-6 from the Stanford University nursery were matched on aggressiveness and watched an adult model behave aggressively or non-aggressively towards a Bobo doll (or saw no model); they were then mildly frustrated and observed through a one-way mirror. Findings: children who saw the aggressive model imitated many of the specific aggressive acts; boys showed more physical aggression, and same-sex models were imitated more Link: observational learning of aggression.

items.stem: Using Berry (1967) as supporting evidence, explain the influence of cultural norms on conformity.
items.answer: Berry (1967). Aim: to investigate whether conformity differs between cultures with different economies. Method: Using an Asch-type line judgement task, Berry compared the conformity of Temne participants in Sierra Leone (a farming society) with Inuit participants on Baffin Island (a hunting society). Findings: the Temne conformed significantly more than the Inuit, which Berry linked to the need for cooperation in food-accumulating societies Link: the influence of cultural norms on conformity.

items.stem: Explain the difference between collectivism and individualism.
items.answer: Individualist cultures emphasise personal goals, independence and personal achievement, while collectivist cultures emphasise group harmony, interdependence and duties to the in-group.
